(1) the relative abundance and behaviour of mixed bacterial populations in oil- and phenolic leachates amended microcosms changed during degradation of phenol, (2) the shifts in the composition and behaviour of mixed population indicated an optimised response of the community to the contaminants present, and (3) the results indicated that the selection of specific bacterial populations in microcosms was a result of the composition of the contaminants present.

(i) the composition of bacterial populations in oil-polluted microcosms is stable and dominated by the same bacterial strain; and (ii) bacterial populations in microcosms polluted by phenolic leachates are more dynamic and the dominant degraders change during the course of bioremediation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behaviour and relative abundances of selected bacterial populations in microcosms and their potential use as inocula for bioremediation.
the development of a new approach to bioaugmentation based on the use of mixed bacterial populations.
the development of a new approach to bioremediation, which involves the use of a mixture of bacterial strains, each of which degrades a particular pollutant.

the behaviour and relative abundances of mixed bacterial populations are dependent on both the composition of the microbial population and on the composition of the environment.
the behaviour of mixed phenol degrading populations in oil- and leachate microsystems differed in terms of the relative abundance of specific bacterial strains and the mode of growth.
the composition of the mixed population is an optimised adaptation to the specific environmental conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in microcosms, a mixed bacterial population with the ability to degrade aromatic compounds was selected and this population was able to optimise the degradation of aromatic contaminants present.
the biodegradation efficiency of the selected populations was dependent on the nature of the contaminants and on their concentration in the medium.
bioaugmentation of polluted soil is a complex process and that the selection of the most suitable bacterial strains to be used for bioremediation should be carefully considered.

the use of mixed populations of bacteria for bioremediation of polluted sites is a promising alternative to the use of single strains.
